translation: She looks at the family, all girls.
The mother, with a child at her breast, awkwardly dismounts the cart and the driver hurries her along because he needs to return to pick up others in the suburbs.
Her backpack falls off her back spilling out some grayish rags and a single string of small, darkened beads.
She gathers them up with embarrassment as if she has just revealed her deepest secrets to the world.
Deymowa passes by and suddenly a boy runs up to her, maybe six or seven years old, looking at her with smiling eyes very content with himself saying: "Praised be Jesus Christ!".
And she automatically but solemnly replies: "Forever and ever, amen".
Tears well up in her eyes as she grabs at her heart.
She kneels down next to the boy clutching his wrists while he continues looking into her tear-filled eyes still wearing that smile on his face; that impish little grin.
The first buildings rise up before them abruptly, without warning.
It seems that the fog changes one's sense of distance, as even Kaśka appears surprised by this.
Suddenly she jumps, tugging at the shafts, and if it hadn't been for Roszek's firm reaction and his whip, she would have overturned the carriage.
Maybe the sparks flying from the forge scared Kaśka or maybe it was the anxious horses waiting their turn to be shoed.
Everywhere the sickly smell of malt lingers, permeating every item on sale.
One could almost fill up on it as if were bread.
The suburb of Rohatyn, Babińce, has a few small breweries that's where that heavy aroma extends from all over the surrounding area.
Many stalls sell beers here, and better stores stock both spirits and mead, mainly trojniak variety.
The store owned by Jewish merchant Wakszul sells winelegitimate Hungarian and Rhenish ones along with somewhat tart ones all the way from Wallachia.
The most would have to be said about the Wolowski family, as it has grown to enormous sizes.
Almost all branches of this family have been ennobled, some were of the Buffalo coat of arms, others were of the On The Helmets coat of arms.
Undoubtedly, Franciszek, the son of Izaak Wolowski the same one that priest Chmielowski called Jeremiah had a great career.
He was born in 1786 in Brünn and raised in Offenbach, he became one of the best lawyers and experts on law at that time.
Interestingly enough when a motion appeared in parliament to grant Polish citizenship to Jews, Franciszek as a deputy argued passionately in his speech that it was not yet time for such move.
First, he said, the Polish nation must regain its independence and only then will it be time for social reforms.
All the Offenbach neophytes were buried in the city cemetery, which after years started to interfere with the plans for city expansion and was eventually liquidated in 1866.
The bones of the people buried there were collected and respectfully reburied elsewhere.
On this occasion, Jakub Frank's skull was exhumed from his grave and, carefully described as "the skull of a Jewish patriarch," ended up in the hands of Offenbach's city historian.
Many years later, under unknown circumstances, it made its way to Berlin where it underwent detailed measurements and examinations; it was deemed an example of Jewish racial inferiority.
After the war, it disappeared without a trace possibly destroyed by wartime chaos; crumbled into dust; or maybe still lying in an underground warehouse of some museum.
After Jakub's death, a time of great peace came for me.
My main occupation became the study of Merkava, to which our conversations with Jeruchim Dembowski were added, as we lived in the same room and grew closer.
I also told Jeruchim about Chai Szor; she was the only woman I could love and did love from that beautiful moment when I had her for one night when I came with news about Jakub to Rohatyn.
But first and foremost, I loved Jakub.
They had been in Iwanie since April.
If it weren't for the good people of Iwanie, they would likely have starved to death.
Iwanie saved their lives and their health, Bejla was now feeling better and no longer coughed as much.
Srol believed that once they were baptized, life would be just as good for them as it was for the Christians.
They would get a piece of land, Bejla could garden vegetables, and he, Srol, could weave rugs because he was good at it.
In old age when their daughters were married off, they'd take them in.
That was all he dreamed of.

Kaśka doesn't want to go.
Roszko says gloomily as the carriage stops.
Roszko gets off the box seat and bids a few vigorous goodbyes.
Then he leans over and peers into the mist, as if he were looking into water.
His shirt is sticking out from beneath his festive red coat, which has faded slightly with wear.
"I don't know where to go," she says.
"How can you not know?
We are already on the Rohatyn high road," says the surprised priest.
Nevertheless!
He gets out of the carriage and follows his servant, walking helplessly around the coach, straining his eyes in the white brightness of surrounding snow.
They think they can see something but their eyes start playing tricks on them when there's nothing for them to latch onto.
How could something like this have happened to them?
It's as if they got lost in their own pocket!
"Quiet!"
The priest suddenly exclaims and raises a finger listening carefully for something in air around him .
Indeed from somewhere on their left side, through clumps of mist rolls in a faint sound of rushing water.
"Follow that noise.
He decides resolutely,"That's running water.
Soon the priest relaxes in his carriage, stretches out his legs, and lets his eyes wander over the sea of fog.
Immediately he falls into thoughtful contemplation for one thinks best when in motion.

Slowly and hesitantly, the mechanism of his mind comes to life; gears begin to turn, setting other wheels in motion, much like the clock on the hallway of his rectory that he purchased from Lviv; it cost him a tidy sum.
Soon there will be a chime.
He starts to wonder if perhaps the world did not emerge from such a fog.

After all, Jewish historian Flavius Josephus claims that world was created during autumn equinox; you might think so because indeed there were fruits in Eden; since an apple hung on a tree it had to be fall.
There's some merit in that thought yet a different idea comes immediately after:
What kind of argument is that?
Couldn't an almighty God create such humble fruits at any time of year?

As they approach the main road leading to Rohatyn, they merge into the stream of pedestrians, riders and carts of all kinds that emerge from the mist, like little figures made out of bread for Christmas.
It's Wednesday, market day in Rohatyn.
Peasant carts loaded with sacks of grain, cages of poultry and various farm products travel along.
Among them briskly march merchants carrying all possible wares; their collapsible stalls expertly folded now rest on their backs like pole bundles.
Soon these will become tables filled with colorful fabrics, wooden toys and eggs collected from villages at a quarter price.
The peasants also lead goats and cows for sale; these animals, terrified by the noise, resist in puddles.

A speeding wagon covered with a holey tarpaulin full of boisterous Jews who gather at Rohatyn's fair from all over passes them by closely followed by an elaborate carriage struggling to maintain its dignity through foggy congestion its shiny lacquer doors marked by mud splatters and its stern driver in a blue cloak looking frustrated;
he apparently didn't anticipate such chaos and is now desperately looking for an opportunity to exit this infernal road.
